chart_gl.title: Accounts 1 — The Chart of Accounts & the General Ledger
chart_gl.desc: The foundation of the finance certification: the GL as the stock ledger's money twin, debit-credit grammar for consultants, chart design as language, account types and their machinery, the posting map of every document, the drill-down culture, and control accounts with their party tie.

lessons.title: Chapter 1 — The second ledger: books that write themselves
lessons.html:
Welcome to the fourth certification — the one the other three kept pointing at. Selling booked revenue, Procurement booked liabilities, Inventory wrote valuation... and every one of those sentences quietly assumed a machine underneath: the accounting layer, where every naira of the firm's life is recorded, organised, and reported. This track is that machine, from its language to its statements.

The two ledgers, twins. Inventory 1 taught the stock ledger — append-only, written only by documents, the firm's stock testimony. The General Ledger (GL) is its money twin: every financial event is a dated entry — account, debit or credit, amount, and the DOCUMENT that caused it — appended forever, edited never, corrections appended beside their mistakes. The two ledgers even write together: the delivery that moved stock wrote a stock entry AND a money entry (the COGS posting — Inventory 5's valuation release, now seen from the money side), and much of this module is learning to see the money shadow every trading document has been casting all along.

The promise: books that write themselves from trade. Here is the sentence that sells this track to every owner and accountant you will ever implement for: in a firm that kept the first three certifications' laws, the books are a by-product of trading properly. The invoice posted revenue, VAT, and the debtor; the receipt posted stock and the creditor accrual; the payment posted the bank — nobody journalised any of it, because the documents carry their accounting inside them. The accountant's job transforms: from writing entries (the bookkeeping treadmill) to GOVERNING the machine — the chart it speaks (this module), the exceptions it needs (module 2), the reconciliations that prove it (module 3), and the statements it produces (module 7). A firm still hand-journalising its sales has not bought less software; it has declined the machine's entire premise — and recognising that situation is a consulting diagnosis you will make often.

What the consultant must hold. You are not becoming an accountant — the boundary from Inventory 5 stands (policy is theirs; machinery is yours) — but you cannot configure, diagnose, or explain the machine without its literacy: the debit-credit grammar (Chapter 2), the chart's design (Chapters 3-4), the posting map (Chapter 5 — which document writes which entries), and the drill-down culture (Chapter 6). That literacy is this module; the rest of the track builds on it exactly as Inventory built on its map. And one orientation before we start: everything here is READ far more often than it is written — the GL is where every question about money ends, and the professionals who can walk it are the ones every meeting goes quiet for.

lessons.title: Chapter 2 — Debits & credits: the grammar, for consultants
lessons.html:
Every GL entry speaks a two-word grammar — debit and credit — and consultants who never learn it spend careers nodding at accountants. One chapter, learned once, permanent.

The equation and the rule. The books balance because they describe one reality twice: Assets = Liabilities + Equity (what the firm HAS equals who has claims on it), with income and expenses as equity's running story. Every event touches at least two accounts, and every entry's debits equal its credits — not as ritual but as arithmetic: money that came from somewhere went somewhere, and the entry records both ends.

The direction table — memorise this, it is the whole grammar:

  • Assets (bank, debtors, stock, equipment): debit to increase, credit to decrease.
  • Expenses (rent, salaries, COGS): debit to increase — expenses behave like assets directionally (both are debits growing), which is the grammar's one merciful simplification.
  • Liabilities (creditors, VAT payable, loans): credit to increase, debit to decrease.
  • Income (sales, other income): credit to increase.
  • Equity (capital, retained earnings): credit to increase.

DEAD is the classic mnemonic — Debits increase Expenses, Assets, Drawings; everything else grows by credit.

The grammar spoken by documents you already know. Read three familiar documents in it, slowly, once: A sales invoice for ₦107,500 (₦100,000 + VAT): DEBIT Debtors ₦107,500 (an asset grew — the customer owes you), CREDIT Sales ₦100,000 (income grew), CREDIT VAT Payable ₦7,500 (a liability grew — FIRS's money in your custody, Selling 6's whole argument now visible as a credit). Debits ₦107,500 = credits ₦107,500. The customer's payment: DEBIT Bank ₦107,500 (asset up), CREDIT Debtors ₦107,500 (asset down — the claim converted to cash). A purchase receipt of stock at ₦940,000: DEBIT Stock ₦940,000 (asset up — Inventory 5's valuation write, money-side), CREDIT the received-not-billed accrual ₦940,000 (a liability grew — you possess goods you have not yet been invoiced for; Chapter 5 completes this thread). Three documents, and the grammar already covers most of trade.

Reading direction in the wild. The practical skills the grammar buys: an account's BALANCE side tells you its health story (Debtors carries a debit balance normally — a CREDIT balance on a customer means you owe THEM: the unallocated advance of Selling 7, now legible in grammar); a P&L account's growth reads directly (credits growing Sales is trade; debits growing Sales is returns and reversals — worth a look when large); and the entry that looks wrong usually IS readable — the expense credited, the income debited, the one-sided-feeling journal — once you ask the grammar's two questions of every line: which family is this account, and did the entry move it the way the story says it should move? That question pair, asked patiently, is how a consultant walks any entry with any accountant as a peer — which is the chapter's entire purpose.

lessons.title: Chapter 3 — The chart as a tree: designing the language
lessons.html:
Every account lives in the Chart of Accounts — and if the shape feels familiar, it should: it is a TREE, with group nodes for reading and ledger (leaf) accounts for posting, and every design law you learned for the warehouse tree transfers with the names changed. This chapter is the design hour.

The structure. Four (or five) root types anchor everything: Assets, Liabilities, Equity, Income, Expenses — the equation's own families, fixed by accounting itself. Beneath them, groups organise for reading (Current Assets → Bank Accounts → the individual banks; Indirect Expenses → Administrative → the specific lines) and ledger accounts — the leaves — take the postings: every GL entry names a LEAF, and posting to a group fails by design (the warehouse-tree refusal, money edition, teaching the same model: money exists in accounts; groups exist so accounts can be read together).

Designing for the firm's reading. The standard chart the system ships is a competent skeleton — the design work is tailoring it to how THIS firm asks questions, and the discipline is Inventory 1's verbatim: start from what must be read, not from what could be listed. The owner's monthly questions (what did we make, what did it cost, where did the money go) define the P&L groups; the statement's needs define the balance-sheet shape; and the granularity rule cuts both ways — an account earns existence when someone will READ its line separately (three bank accounts are three leaves because three reconciliations; Office Expenses splitting into eleven micro-accounts nobody reads separately is sprawl), and a distinction nobody reads is carried by a DIMENSION, not an account (the branch, the service line — module 6's terrain, previewed: the chart answers WHAT KIND of money; dimensions answer WHOSE and WHERE — conflating them is how charts explode into per-branch copies of every expense line, the disease module 6 exists to cure).

Naming and numbering for the decade. The conventions law, fourth appearance: names that read plainly in every report forever (the accountant's vocabulary, not the software's), numbering where the firm's reporting tradition uses it (consistent, gapped for insertion, never re-used), and the shape SHALLOW — two to three levels below root serves almost every trading firm, and the five-level chart is the five-level warehouse tree: bureaucracy nobody navigates.

Change discipline. Charts live for decades, and their change rules mirror the item master's: renaming a leaf is cheap (the history follows the account); restructuring — re-parenting groups, merging accounts — is an event (merging accounts merges their histories irreversibly; the annual review is its editing room); and retiring follows the delisting flow (balance cleared deliberately, then disabled — never deleted: the GL's testimony includes retired witnesses, the same sentence as every ledger in this academy because it is the same law). The chart walk happens at implementation WITH the accountant — their language, their statements, their sign-off — and annually thereafter; a chart nobody has walked in five years reads like a house nobody has cleaned: functional, and full of rooms no one can explain.

lessons.title: Chapter 4 — Account types: the machinery behind the leaves
lessons.html:
Two leaves can sit side by side in the tree and behave completely differently — because beneath the tree position sits the account type, and the type is what wires an account into the system's machinery. This chapter is the wiring diagram.

  • Bank and Cash — accounts of these types join the payment machinery (payment modes point at them — the mode-to-account mapping both money tracks used) and, decisively, the bank reconciliation (module 3's whole subject): a real-world bank account modelled as anything but a Bank-type account is invisible to the reconciliation that proves it.
  • Receivable and Payable — the control accounts: entries here DEMAND a party (the customer or supplier), which is what makes the per-party ledgers of both money tracks possible — the control account is the total, the party dimension is the detail, and their permanent agreement is module 4's law (Chapter 7 previews it). An invoice posting to a non-Receivable account has left the machinery that ages, allocates, and statements — which is why the type, not the name, is what matters.
  • Stock — the accounts the perpetual-inventory machinery writes (Inventory 5's valuation, landing here): stock-in-hand by warehouse grouping where configured, the received-not-billed accrual, the stock adjustment homes. Manual journals against Stock-type accounts are fenced precisely because two machines (the stock ledger and the GL) must agree — the bridge of Inventory 5, protected at the type level.
  • Tax — the VAT and WHT accounts the templates post to (Selling 6, Procurement 7): typed so the tax machinery and its reports can find them, reconciled monthly against their registers by the rituals both tracks installed.
  • Depreciation, Fixed Asset, Accumulated Depreciation — the asset machinery's accounts (module 7 gives fixed assets their overview).
  • Round-off, exchange gain/loss, opening temporary accounts — the system's designated homes for its own arithmetic edges: configured once, reviewed for reasonableness (a growing round-off account is a symptom, not a rounding).

The type discipline. Three rules carry the chapter: type at creation — set correctly when the account is born, because retyping an account with history is an event bordering on migration (the receivable that spent a year untyped has a year of party-less entries no toggle repairs); machinery over cosmetics — when a posting misbehaves (the invoice that will not take a party, the bank missing from reconciliation), the TYPE is the first suspect, before names, before permissions; and defaults complete the wiring — the company's default accounts (debtors, creditors, stock accounts, round-off, the mode mappings) are where documents learn which leaves to write, and the settings walk that reviews them is the same constitutional hour as every settings walk in this academy: each default read as the policy it is, recorded, and re-walked annually.

lessons.title: Chapter 5 — The posting map: what every document writes
lessons.html:
The academy's central promise — books that write themselves — becomes concrete here: the posting map, document by document. Learn it once and every GL mystery becomes a lookup; this is the reference card of the entire track.

  • Sales Invoice — DR Debtors (party: the customer) for the gross; CR Sales income for the net; CR VAT Payable for the tax (the template's account). With Update Stock on (the POS-style flow): also CR Stock, DR COGS — the invoice doing the delivery's money work because it did the delivery's stock work.
  • Delivery Note — the stock movement's money shadow: CR Stock (value leaves at the method's figure — Inventory 5's release), DR COGS. No revenue here: the timeline law's accounting face — delivery moves value, invoicing books revenue — and the reason a period's deliveries and invoices must both be complete for its margin to be true (module 7's cut-off discipline, seeded now).
  • Payment Entry (received) — DR Bank (the mode's account); CR Debtors (party) — the claim becomes cash. Deductions ride as extra lines: the WHT-at-source receivable (Selling 7's ₦50k) debits its asset account in the same entry.
  • Purchase Receipt — DR Stock at landed valuation (Inventory 5's write, money-side); CR Stock Received But Not Billed — the accrual that says we possess what we have not yet been invoiced for: the three-way match's accounting shadow, and the account whose balance IS the open match queue in naira (a beautiful diagnostic: an old, large RNB balance is Procurement 7's To-Bill list aging, read from the GL side).
  • Purchase Invoice — CR Creditors (party: the supplier); DR the RNB accrual (clearing it — possession now billed); DR Input VAT (the claimable asset). Where no receipt preceded (the service invoice, the exempted tail): DR the expense account directly. WHT withheld posts its CR to WHT Payable inside the payment entry that settles it (Procurement 7's ₦50k, now grammatical).
  • Stock Entries — issues and write-offs: CR Stock, DR the expense home the attribution names (Inventory 2's landing); Material Receipts: DR Stock, CR the designated offset (the accountant's policy from Inventory 2, here as an account); transfers: silent in the P&L (value travels, nothing is earned or consumed — one Stock debit, one Stock credit where warehouse-level accounts apply, or nothing at all where one account serves).
  • Stock Reconciliation — the adjustment's money face: DR/CR Stock against the adjustment home — the shrinkage number of Inventory 4, landing in the P&L where the accountant directed.
  • Journal Entry — whatever it says, which is exactly its power and its danger: module 2's entire subject.

Using the map. Three habits: verify at go-live — one live document of each kind, its GL entries pulled and read against the map (the hour that catches the mis-wired default before a month of postings inherits it); diagnose by footprint — the strange balance decomposes into documents, and each document's footprint tells you instantly whether IT behaved (the RNB that never clears is invoices bypassing receipts; the COGS that posts at invoice AND delivery is Update Stock double-wired); and teach it — the client accountant who holds this map stops fearing the system and starts governing it, which is the implementation outcome everything else serves.

lessons.title: Chapter 6 — Reading the GL: the drill-down culture
lessons.html:
The General Ledger report is the track's stock-ledger-walk: the diagnostic read that answers HOW any balance got this way. This chapter is the reading craft — and the culture it builds.

The report. The GL, filtered: by account (the account's full story between dates — opening balance, every entry, closing balance), by party (a customer or supplier ACROSS accounts — their whole financial relationship on one screen, the accounts-chair version of the account screens both money tracks built), by voucher (one document's complete footprint — the posting map verified live), by cost center or dimension (module 6's lens, previewed). Each entry carries its date, accounts, amounts, party, remarks — and its DOCUMENT, which is the whole point.

The drill. The provenance culture of Inventory 7, now at its origin: statement line → account balance → GL entries → the document → its attachments and chain. Three or four clicks from any number on any report to the paper that caused it — and the reading discipline is to USE them: the disputed figure opened live in the meeting, the strange balance walked to its entries, the month-end query answered with a filtered GL instead of a recollection. The consultant models this relentlessly at implementation, because the culture sets in the first month: the firm whose managers drill down argues from documents; the firm whose managers export argues from tabs — the Inventory 7 sentence, repeated because the GL is where it matters most.

The trial balance, introduced. The GL's summary face: every account, its period debits, credits, and closing balance — necessarily balancing (the grammar guarantees it), and read not for its balance (which is arithmetic) but for its ANOMALIES: the account that should be zero and is not (the RNB aging, the suspense with a squatter, the round-off growing), the balance on the wrong side (the credit-balance customer, the debit-balance VAT payable — each a story the grammar makes legible), the account nobody recognises (Chapter 9's pattern). The monthly trial-balance scan — ten minutes, anomalies flagged — is the accounts layer's cycle count: small, rhythmic, and the reason year-end holds no surprises. Module 7 gives the close its full ritual; the scan is its daily-wear version.

Reading with the grammar. The chapter closes where Chapter 2 opened: the GL rewards the literate. The balance-side read (which side does this account normally carry, and is it there?), the growth read (what has been increasing this account, and should it?), the counterparty read (every entry has another side — where did the other half go?): three questions, asked of any account, that turn the ledger from a wall of numbers into a narrative — and the consultant who narrates it aloud while drilling (this is the invoice, here is its VAT line, that credit is the payment allocating) is training every listener into the culture at once. The GL is the firm's money autobiography; this track exists to make you one of its fluent readers.

lessons.title: Chapter 7 — Control accounts & party ledgers: the tie
lessons.html:
One idea deserves its own chapter before module 4 builds on it, because it is the accounts layer's version of a law every prior track taught: the control account and its subledger, and the tie that makes both trustworthy.

The structure. Debtors is ONE leaf in the chart — one balance, the total of every customer's claim. But every entry to it carried a PARTY (Chapter 4's type machinery), so the system maintains, in effect, a ledger per customer INSIDE the account: the party filter on the GL is the customer's statement; the receivables report ages the parties; and the control account's balance is, by construction, the sum of its parties' balances. The same structure serves Creditors, and the pattern generalises: the control is the total; the subledger is the detail; the machinery keeps them agreeing because they are the same entries read two ways.

Why the tie is a law. The agreement holds automatically — UNTIL someone posts around the machinery: the journal entry to Debtors without a party (a naira in the control that belongs to no customer — the total now exceeds the details, and every customer statement is silently suspect), the balance corrected at the control level while the party detail stands (the reverse divergence), the migration that loaded totals without parties. Once diverged, the control-to-subledger reconciliation is archaeology — which is why the discipline is prevention: party-typed accounts take party-carrying entries only (the system enforces most of it; module 2's journal governance fences the rest), and the monthly tie check — control balance against the party report's total, agreeing to the kobo — joins the close's checklist as the third bridge of the academy (stock-to-accounts from Inventory 5; the two tax registers from the money tracks; now debtors and creditors to their parties). Three bridges, one principle: a total the details cannot reproduce is a total nobody should trust.

What the tie buys, operationally. With it intact: the ageing reports are believed (collections and the payment run both work from them — Selling 7 and Procurement 7's machinery standing on this floor); customer and supplier statements go out without fear (the statement IS the party ledger, printed); the auditor samples parties and finds the control every time (the confirmation exercise that ends early); and the balance-sheet's receivables line is a number with 400 defensible components rather than one asserted total. The subledger disciplines both money tracks taught — allocation, advances matched, references carried — were, from this chair, tie-maintenance all along: every unallocated payment and orphaned advance is a party whose detail has stopped telling the control's story cleanly.

The consultant's preview of module 4. This chapter is deliberately the foundation only: module 4 operates the chair — provisioning and bad debts, the advance machinery from the accounts side, statements and confirmations, the migration disciplines that load parties correctly. What must be permanent from today: when any receivables or payables number is questioned, the FIRST check is the tie — control against parties — because every deeper diagnosis depends on knowing whether the two still tell one story.

lessons.title: Chapter 8 — Case study: HealthTrade's chart is born
lessons.html:
The accountant, the consultant, and one afternoon: HealthTrade's accounting constitution, designed as Chapters 1-7 taught it. Every step names its chapter.

Step 1 — the reading list first (Ch. 3). Before an account is touched, the MD's monthly questions are written down: sales and margin (by branch, eventually — noted for module 6), what running the firm costs (rent, people, power, logistics — read separately), what the firm owns and owes (banks by account, stock, debtors, creditors, the tax custodies). The accountant adds the statement's needs and the audit's. The list — fifteen questions — becomes the chart's specification: start from what must be read.

Step 2 — tailoring the skeleton (Ch. 3-4). The standard chart is walked against the list: the three real banks become three Bank-type leaves under Bank Accounts (three reconciliations coming — module 3); Debtors and Creditors confirmed as typed controls; the Stock family confirmed wired to the perpetual machinery (the Inventory 5 bridge's other end); the tax custodies named plainly — VAT Payable, Input VAT, WHT Payable, WHT Receivable (four accounts whose stories three tracks already taught); expense groups shaped to the reading list (eleven micro-splits of admin collapsed to four lines someone will actually read); and the branch question answered the RIGHT way: NOT per-branch expense copies, but the dimension noted for module 6 — the chart stays one language; the branches become a lens. Names in the accountant's vocabulary; numbering per their tradition; two levels below root, nowhere three.

Step 3 — the posting map verified live (Ch. 5). One of each document, real, small, and walked: a test invoice's entries read aloud against the map (Debtors gross, Sales net, VAT Payable — the accountant nodding at the grammar); a receipt's RNB accrual explained (this balance IS your unbilled possession — watch it clear when the invoice books); a delivery's COGS line tied to Inventory 5's valuation (the stock module priced it; this entry released it); a payment's allocation read in the party ledger. Two defaults corrected on the spot — the round-off account pointed at a sensible home, one payment mode mapped to the wrong bank — the hour doing exactly what Chapter 5 promised: catching the mis-wire before a month inherits it.

Step 4 — the first reads (Ch. 6-7). The GL drilled live for the accountant: statement → account → entries → document, four clicks, narrated. The trial balance scanned — one anomaly found and enjoyed: a small credit balance on a customer, drilled to an unallocated advance from the go-live week, allocated on the spot (the tie's first save). The monthly rhythm agreed before the afternoon ends: the trial-balance scan, the three bridges (stock-to-accounts, tax registers, control-to-parties), and the GL open in every meeting where a number is disputed. The accountant leaves governing a machine instead of feeding one — and the afternoon's last sentence is the track's thesis, said back to the consultant unprompted: so the books write themselves, and my job is to keep them honest.

lessons.title: Chapter 9 — Common mistakes & the first law
lessons.html:
The chart-and-ledger layer's scar tissue — the design mistakes that surface as everyone's confusion for years. Symptom → disease → fix.

Pattern 1 — chart sprawl. Symptom: four hundred accounts for an eleven-person firm; nobody can say what half are for; every report is a scroll. Disease: accounts created per whim — one per project, per branch, per mood (Ch. 3) — the warehouse-sprawl twin, and the same dilution: a language with four hundred words nobody speaks. Fix: the reading test applied ruthlessly in a consolidation pass (balances merged by documented entries into accounts that are read; husks retired through the flow), creation rights narrowed, and dimensions carrying the distinctions that were never account-shaped.

Pattern 2 — the suspense squatter. Symptom: a suspense or miscellaneous account with a large, aging, growing balance. Disease: the account meant for momentary parking used as a destination (Ch. 3, 6) — every entry someone couldn't classify, accumulating into a number that means we don't know. Fix: suspense swept to zero monthly as a close-checklist line (each squatter classified to its true home), and the classification gaps that fed it fixed at their source — a default, a template, or a training.

Pattern 3 — the untyped leaf. Symptom: the bank missing from reconciliation; the invoice refusing a party; receivables that cannot age. Disease: accounts created with names instead of types (Ch. 4) — the machinery wired to types, the leaf invisible to it. Fix: type at creation as law; the retype-with-history treated as the event it is; and the type audit (every Bank-type against the real bank list, every control against its party machinery) in the annual chart walk.

Pattern 4 — the partyless posting. Symptom: the control disagreeing with its parties; customer statements missing money everyone knows exists. Disease: entries to control accounts without parties — journals around the machinery (Ch. 7; module 2 owns the fence). Fix: the divergence reconciled once (archaeology, priced honestly), the journal governance installed, and the monthly tie check standing guard after.

Pattern 5 — the account nobody can explain. Symptom: the trial balance line that draws blank looks in the meeting. Disease: the chart accumulated instead of designed (Ch. 3) — history's sediment presented as structure. Fix: the annual walk with the accountant, each unexplainable account investigated to its entries (the GL always knows), then merged, retired, or documented — a chart where every line has a one-sentence explanation is the deliverable.

The first law. Selling's laws began with masters; Procurement's with the supply base; Inventory's with the map. This track's begins with the language: the chart of accounts is the language of the business — every naira speaks through an account, the tree is designed from what must be read, and the ledger beneath it is append-only testimony written by documents. Learn the grammar, design the language, wire the types, hold the posting map, drill everything to its paper, and keep the controls tied to their parties. Seven modules stand on this floor; module 2 opens the one door this module kept locked: the journal entry, where humans write the ledger directly — and the governance that keeps that power honest.

lessons.title: Chapter 1 — The one door: direct writing and its dangers
lessons.html:
Module 1 celebrated a ledger written by documents; this module opens the exception: the Journal Entry — the document whose only job is to write the GL DIRECTLY, any accounts, any amounts, whatever its author says. It exists because real accounting needs it (Chapter 3's catalogue is genuine and monthly); it is dangerous because of what it bypasses — and holding both truths at once is this module.

What the journal bypasses. Every trading document carries machinery around its GL posting: the invoice maintained the party subledger, fed the VAT register, and aged into collections; the receipt wrote the stock ledger beside the money; the payment allocated against its references. The journal carries NONE of it — it writes naked GL lines, and every naira it posts is a naira that skipped the systems that make totals decomposable: the party tie (module 1's third bridge), the stock bridge, the tax registers, the match queue. A journal is not wrong for this — it is SPECIALISED for events that have no trading document (rent accruing, depreciation charging) — but the specialisation cuts both ways: used where a document exists, the journal fixes the GL's number while breaking every detail beneath it, and the break is silent: the trial balance still balances, the statements still print, and the divergence surfaces weeks later as a tie that will not reconcile. This — not fraud, mere convenience — is how most books rot.

The law, previewed. The module's discipline in one sentence, stated now and earned across nine chapters: the journal is the exception and the document is the rule — what a document can do, a document must do. Sales are invoiced, never journalised (the revenue journal breaks VAT, the subledger, and the statement at once — Chapter 6 itemises it); purchases are billed; stock moves by stock documents; payments are payment entries. The journal takes what remains: the genuine catalogue of Chapter 3, governed by Chapter 7's narrow door.

The consultant's stance. You will meet the journal habit constantly — the accountant trained on manual books who journalises everything, the firm whose system is a GL with ten thousand journals and no trading documents at all (module 1's diagnosis: the machine's premise declined). The stance is respectful and firm: the habit is not incompetence — it is fluency in the OLD instrument — and the implementation's job is transferring that fluency to the machine: every recurring journal examined for the document that should replace it, every correction routed through Chapter 5's doctrine, and the journal count itself watched as a health metric — a trading firm's monthly journals should be countable on hands (the recurring set plus a few events), and a rising count is the machine being quietly declined one entry at a time.

lessons.title: Chapter 2 — Anatomy of a journal entry
lessons.html:
The instrument itself, field by field — because the journal's governance (Chapter 7) enforces disciplines that live in these fields, and a consultant must know exactly where.

  • The rows — each row an account, a debit OR credit amount, and the row-level extras the account's type demands: the party where the account is a Receivable/Payable control (module 1's tie, enforced at entry — a journal CAN lawfully touch Debtors, but only carrying the customer it concerns, and Chapter 6 narrows even that), the cost center or dimension where P&L accounts want their address (module 6's terrain — the journal that charges an expense must still say whose expense), and reference fields where rows settle against existing entries.
  • The balance law — total debits equal total credits or the entry will not save: the grammar's arithmetic (module 1) enforced structurally. A journal that needs to be one-sided is a misdiagnosis — the other side exists; the author has not found it yet, and suspense is not the answer (Chapter 9 convicts the parking habit).
  • Posting date — WHEN the entry speaks: the chronology law in its accounts vocabulary. Honest dates always (the accrual for March dated in March), the frozen-period discipline governing the past (the accounts settings' close guards — module 8 formalises; the Inventory 2 freeze logic already taught it), and the reversal-dated-forward pattern for accrual unwinding (Chapter 4).
  • Entry type — the classification field: Journal Entry, Bank Entry, Cash Entry, Contra Entry (bank-to-bank and cash-to-bank movements — module 3 uses these), Credit Note / Debit Note journals, Depreciation Entry, and the rest. The type does light machinery work (contra entries join the bank reconciliation's world) and heavy REVIEW work: the monthly journal audit (Chapter 7) reads by type, and a mis-typed entry hides from its reviewer.
  • Reference number and date — the external anchor: the bank advice, the payroll summary, the agreement clause — the paper the journal answers to.
  • Remarks — the story field, and the module's most enforced discipline: every journal narrates itself — what happened, why this entry, what evidence supports it. The trading documents carry their stories structurally (an invoice IS its own explanation); the journal's story lives only here, and a journal whose remarks are empty is testimony without a witness: six months later, nobody — including its author — can say why it exists, and the audit (external or internal) treats it exactly as it deserves. The remarks law has no exceptions; the recurring templates (Chapter 7) carry their stories pre-written.

Reading a journal like a reviewer. The five-question scan the monthly audit applies, learnable now: WHO wrote it (author against the permission list), WHAT does it touch (any forbidden accounts — Chapter 6), WHICH WAY (the grammar check: does the story match the directions?), WHEN (honest date? open period?), and WHY (do the remarks and reference actually explain it?). Five questions, thirty seconds per entry — and the entries that fail them are precisely the ones worth the second look.

lessons.title: Chapter 3 — The lawful catalogue
lessons.html:
What SHOULD be a journal — the genuine list, itemised, because the discipline of Chapter 1 only holds if the exceptions are named rather than negotiated case by case. A trading firm's lawful journal traffic:

  • Accruals and prepayments — the matching principle's instruments (Chapter 4's whole subject): expenses spread to the periods that consumed them, income deferred to the periods that earned it. The largest lawful category, and monthly by nature.
  • Payroll — the salary journal from the payroll summary: DR salary expense (by department/dimension), CR net-pay liability (cleared by the payment run), CR the statutory custodies — PAYE, pension, other deductions — each a liability account whose custody logic is Selling 6's VAT argument again: withheld money is held, not owned (module 5 gives the Nigerian statutory picture its own chapter). Where a payroll module automates this, the journal is machine-written; the consultant still reads it against the map once.
  • Depreciation — the periodic charge: DR depreciation expense, CR accumulated depreciation — machine-written where the fixed-asset machinery runs (module 7's overview), a governed monthly journal where it does not yet.
  • Bank charges, interest, and bank-side events — the charges the statement reveals (module 3's reconciliation feeds these): DR bank charges, CR bank — journalised as Bank Entries with the statement as reference, and only ever FROM the reconciliation ritual, not from memory.
  • Opening balances — the go-live set piece (the accounts twin of Inventory 4's opening): governed, evidenced, accountant-signed, and loaded once — with the party-level and document-level disciplines module 4 details (opening debtors loaded as per-party, per-invoice detail, never one blob to a control — the tie must be born intact, exactly as batch identity had to be).
  • Owner and inter-entity movements — capital introduced, drawings, director loans, movements between related entities: real events with no trading document, journalised with the evidence referenced — and flagged early as the category MOST needing the accountant's policy hand (the tax and legal shape of owner movements is their terrain; yours is ensuring the entries carry parties, stories, and consistency).
  • Corrections — lawful under the doctrine, and only under it (Chapter 5).

The catalogue's edge. Two tests decide whether a proposed journal belongs: the document test — does a trading document exist for this event? (If yes, the journal is forbidden regardless of convenience — the sale, the purchase, the stock move, the payment all have documents, and Chapter 6 shows what each substitution breaks.) And the story test — can the remarks state a real-world event with evidence? (A journal that exists to make a number right rather than to record something that happened is not an entry; it is an override wearing one — the reconciliation-as-eraser conviction of Inventory 4, arrived at the GL.) The catalogue plus the two tests is the whole law; everything after is mechanics and governance.

lessons.title: Chapter 4 — Accruals & prepayments: matching, worked
lessons.html:
The lawful catalogue's largest resident deserves its own chapter — because matching is the accounting idea consultants most need to hold fluently, and because its journals are the recurring set every implementation builds.

The principle. The P&L's job is to state what a period EARNED and what it CONSUMED — not what it happened to pay. Cash timing and economic timing diverge constantly (rent paid yearly, consumed monthly; power consumed now, billed next month), and the accrual/prepayment machinery is how the books keep the two honest: the payment's date is a bank fact; the expense's date is a consumption fact; matching books each on its own date. Without it, margins lurch with payment calendars — the January that carries the whole year's rent, the fat months where no bills arrived — and every monthly read the academy has built (the health pages, the MD conversations) reads noise.

Prepayment, worked. HealthTrade pays annual rent of ₦2,400,000 in January. The payment entry: DR Prepaid Rent (an ASSET — eleven months of future occupancy is a thing the firm owns) ₦2,400,000, CR Bank. Then the monthly journal, twelve times: DR Rent Expense ₦200,000, CR Prepaid Rent ₦200,000 — each month consuming one-twelfth of the asset into expense. January's P&L carries ₦200,000 of rent, not ₦2.4m; December's carries its ₦200,000 from cash paid a year earlier; and the Prepaid Rent balance at any month IS the occupancy still owed — a balance-sheet line that means something, which is the pattern's quiet elegance. The recurring template (Chapter 7) writes this without anyone remembering; the annual payment refreshes the asset; and the same shape serves insurance, licences, subscriptions — anything paid ahead of its consumption.

Accrual, worked. The mirror: March consumes ₦180,000 of diesel and power, but the bills arrive in April. March's close journals: DR Utilities Expense ₦180,000, CR Accrued Expenses (a liability — the firm owes for what it consumed) — March's P&L now tells March's truth. The reversal pattern completes it: the accrual REVERSES on April 1st (the system's auto-reversal serves exactly this), so when April's actual bills post through their proper documents, the net lands clean — the estimate cleared, the actuals standing, no double-count. The estimate-reverse-actual rhythm is the accountant's monthly craft; the consultant's job is the template, the reversal wiring, and the close-checklist line that asks which consumptions have no bills yet?

The income side. The mirror mirrored: cash received AHEAD of earning is not income — it is a liability (unearned/deferred revenue: the annual service contract billed in advance, the customer deposit for undelivered goods — Selling 7's advances, now with their accounting name). The recognition journal moves it to income as the earning happens (monthly for the service contract; at delivery for the deposit — where the trading documents' own advance machinery does it, the machinery wins per the document test, and the journal serves only the shapes the documents don't). The direction discipline matters commercially: deferred income overstated understates this year and flatters next; recognised early it manufactures profit that hasn't happened — which is why the recognition schedule is the ACCOUNTANT'S policy, written down, and the journals merely execute it.

Sizing honestly. Matching is proportionate: the eleven-person firm accrues the material items (rent, payroll-adjacent, the big utilities) and lets kobo-level timing ride; the audited firm matches comprehensively. The threshold is policy, set with the accountant — but the PATTERN is universal, because a monthly P&L that lurches with payment timing is unreadable at any size, and readable months are what the whole reading culture stands on.

lessons.title: Chapter 5 — The correction doctrine: never edit history
lessons.html:
Mistakes happen — the wrong account, the wrong amount, the wrong month — and what separates clean books from archaeological sites is the correction DOCTRINE. One chapter, four rules, no exceptions.

Rule 1 — history is never edited. The append-only law, now at the ledger where it matters most: a posted entry is testimony, and testimony is not rewritten — it is answered. Corrections are NEW entries that reverse and restate, standing beside the mistake forever, telling the full story: error, discovery, repair. The instinct to just fix the posted entry — even where permissions technically allow amendment — is the instinct to make the books lie about their own past, and every stakeholder who audits, reconciles, or trusts the ledger depends on it never happening.

Rule 2 — the reversal-and-repost pattern. The mechanical form: a reversing entry (the original's exact mirror — same accounts, same amounts, directions flipped; the system's reverse function builds it) kills the mistake's effect; a fresh entry posts the truth. Both carry references to the original and to each other, and remarks that narrate (reversal of JV-0231, expense posted to wrong account; see JV-0233 for correct posting). The GL now reads: mistake, mirror, truth — three entries, one honest story, and any reviewer reconstructs it in a minute.

Rule 3 — documents are corrected as documents. The doctrine's most-violated rule, and the one that protects everything module 1 built: when the ERROR lives in a trading document — the invoice with the wrong customer, the receipt with the wrong quantity, the payment against the wrong reference — the correction happens at the DOCUMENT (cancel-and-amend where the chain allows; the returns and note machinery where trade has moved on — every trading track taught its own correction paths), and NEVER as a journal patching the GL around it. The journal-patch is the module's signature disease: it fixes the balance while the document still tells the old story — so the party subledger, the stock ledger, the tax register, and the match queue all disagree with the GL that looks right, and the three bridges (module 1) begin their slow divergence. The diagnostic follows: a tie that will not reconcile almost always has a journal in it — and the audit's fastest tool is filtering journals against control, stock, tax, and bank accounts, where honest traffic is nearly zero.

Rule 4 — period discipline governs WHEN. The error found in an open month corrects in that month, honest-dated. The error found after close corrects in the CURRENT period with remarks naming the original date (reported truth stays reported — the frozen-past law of Inventory 8, verbatim), unless materiality forces the accountant's formal reopening decision — theirs, eventful, documented. The correction that quietly backdates into a closed month to make the reports right has made every circulated report wrong instead, which is the trade nobody sane accepts once it is said out loud.

The correction file. Material corrections carry their working — what was wrong, how found, what fixed, references end to end — the Inventory 4 investigation file, GL edition. And the aggregate READ: corrections by cause, quarterly, because a ledger needing the same correction monthly has an upstream disease (a default mis-wired, a template wrong, a training gap), and the correction log is where it shows first. Fix the cause; the corrections fall; the books quiet down — the pattern every track has taught, closing its loop in the GL.

lessons.title: Chapter 6 — The forbidden list: what each journal breaks
lessons.html:
Some journals are not governed — they are forbidden, because each one breaks a machine that cannot tell you it is broken. The list, with each entry's what breaks, is the module's fence — teach it verbatim.

  • Revenue journals replacing invoices. DR Debtors, CR Sales, no invoice. Breaks: the VAT register (output tax unbooked or untracked — a compliance failure, not a style choice), the party subledger's document trail (a balance with no invoice to allocate, dispute, or statement), collections (nothing to age properly), and e-invoicing obligations where they apply. The sale has a document; the document is the law. Same conviction, purchase side: expense journals replacing supplier invoices break input VAT, WHT capture, and the creditor's ledger at once.
  • Journals to Stock accounts. Breaks: the stock-to-accounts bridge — the GL moves, the stock ledger does not, and Inventory 5's continuous agreement dies by exactly the journal's amount, permanently, until someone excavates. Stock value is wrong? The error is a stock DOCUMENT (a receipt's rate, a missing entry, a reconciliation) — find it and fix it there; the fence around Stock-type accounts (module 1) exists for this paragraph.
  • Journals to control accounts without parties — and mostly, at all. The party-less journal breaks the tie outright (module 1's third bridge — a naira belonging to no customer). But even the party-carrying journal to Debtors or Creditors deserves suspicion: the events it usually claims (write-off, discount, settlement adjustment) have PROPER instruments — credit and debit notes, the payment deduction machinery, the bad-debt provisioning of module 4 — that carry tax and subledger consequences the naked journal skips. The rule of thumb the governance enforces: control-account journals are rare, party-carrying, and second-signed — or they are the disease.
  • Journals to tax accounts outside the ritual. Breaks: the register agreement — VAT Payable that no longer equals the invoice register's story, WHT accounts that no longer tie to certificates (the money tracks' monthly reconciliations both stand on register-to-account agreement). Tax accounts move by documents and by the filing/remittance ritual's entries; the adjusting journal that makes the account match a filing someone computed OUTSIDE the system is the tail wagging the dog — reconcile the register, find the divergence, fix its document.
  • Journals to bank accounts outside real bank events. Breaks: the reconciliation (module 3) — the GL bank balance acquires a line the statement will never show, and the reconciliation carries an unexplainable difference forever after. Bank accounts move when the BANK moved; the statement is the witness, and Chapter 3's bank-side entries (charges, interest) post FROM the reconciliation, referenced to it.

The pattern beneath the list. Every forbidden journal shares one anatomy: it writes the GL's TOTAL while skipping the DETAIL system that total answers to — and module 1's law names the crime: a total the details cannot reproduce is a total nobody should trust. The forbidden list is not accounting conservatism; it is the defence of every bridge, register, and tie the academy spent three tracks building — one fence, five gates, taught once and enforced by Chapter 7's door.

lessons.title: Chapter 7 — Journal governance: the narrow door
lessons.html:
The manual layer's power gets the treatment every dangerous power in this academy has received: named holders, structural review, and a rhythm that reads it. The governance chapter.

Who may journal. Narrow — the accountant and a named backstop (two names, the Inventory 8 pattern: two PEOPLE, not two departments), never warehouse or sales operators, never branch managers (their corrections route through documents and requests, not direct GL access). The permission maps to the reality that a journal can move any naira anywhere: it is the accounts layer's adjust permission — the reconciliation's GL twin — and it earns the same two-names discipline for the same reason: the day everyone holds the pen, every fence in Chapter 6 is a suggestion.

Thresholds and second eyes. Value thresholds route large journals to a second sign-off even between the two names (the submission workflow carries it), and certain CATEGORIES are second-signed regardless of value: anything touching control accounts (Chapter 6's rare-and-party-carrying rule enforced as workflow), opening and closing entries, and corrections above the materiality line. The threshold numbers are the client's, written in the policy page like every gate number in every track.

The recurring set — templates, not memory. The lawful monthly traffic (Chapter 3-4's accruals, prepayment consumptions, payroll, depreciation) is built ONCE as templates: accounts pre-wired, dimensions pre-set, stories pre-written, amounts updated per period (or auto-generated where the machinery serves). The template set is the manual layer's honest census — a trading firm's recurring journals fit on one page — and everything OUTSIDE the set is, by construction, an event: visible, reviewable, and asked about. The design converts the audit question from are these thousand journals right? to the recurring set ran; what are these six others? — which is the whole game.

The monthly journal audit. The close checklist's standing line (module 7 will place it): every journal of the month, listed, scanned by the five questions of Chapter 2 — author, accounts, direction, date, story. Ten to twenty minutes at a healthy firm (the count is small — Chapter 1's health metric), and the read has teeth in both directions: the individual catch (the forbidden account touched, the empty remarks, the date that wandered) and the AGGREGATE tells (the journal count trending up — the machine being declined; the same correction repeating — the upstream disease of Chapter 5; one author's entries clustering at period-end — the pattern that deserves a conversation before it deserves a name). The audit is also where the correction log (Chapter 5) and the suspense sweep (module 1's checklist line) live — one sitting, three reads, the manual layer held honest.

Governance sized honestly. The eleven-person firm: the accountant journals, the founder second-signs above the threshold, the template set runs, the monthly audit is fifteen minutes with coffee. The audited enterprise: workflow-enforced approvals, segregated preparation and posting, the audit formalised. Same shape, same fences, same two-names core — the academy's sizing law, applied to the pen.

lessons.title: Chapter 8 — Case study: HealthTrade's manual layer
lessons.html:
The month the manual layer was built — and the three tests that proved it. Every chapter clocks in.

The recurring set built (Ch. 3-4, 7). The consultant and the accountant census the firm's genuine journal traffic and build the templates in an afternoon: the rent prepayment (₦2.4m January payment to Prepaid Rent; the ₦200k monthly consumption template, story pre-written, twelve months scheduled); the payroll journal (from the payroll summary: salary expense by dimension, net-pay liability, PAYE and pension custodies — the accountant walking the consultant through the statutory lines, the consultant wiring the template and flagging module 5's coming deep-dive); the utilities accrual (month-end estimate, auto-reversing on the 1st — the estimate-reverse-actual rhythm demonstrated live across March/April: March's ₦180k accrual, April's reversal, April's actual bills posting through their purchase documents, the net landing clean and the accountant, seeing the reversal pattern work for the first time, adopting it for two more accrual lines unprompted); and depreciation (a governed monthly journal now; the fixed-asset automation noted for module 7). The census closes at seven recurring templates — one page, as promised.

A correction done right (Ch. 5). Week three: February's generator maintenance — ₦340,000 — discovered posted to Repairs when the policy wants it in a dedicated Generator Running Costs line the MD reads separately (the chart's reading list at work). The temptation — edit the posted journal — is declined out loud, as teaching: instead, the mirror reversal (referenced to the original), the fresh posting to the right account (referenced to both), remarks narrating all three. The GL reads mistake-mirror-truth; the drill-down from the MD's generator line tells the whole story in four clicks; and the accountant's comment closes the lesson: the books now remember the mistake AND the repair — that is what makes them believable.

A forbidden journal refused (Ch. 6). Week four: a branch manager calls the accountant directly — a customer is disputing ₦86,000, just adjust the debtor and we'll sort it later. The refusal is the fence working: the party-carrying journal to Debtors would move the control while no document tells the customer's ledger WHY — the statement would show a naked adjustment, the dispute would lose its paper trail, and later never comes. The routing instead: the dispute investigated (Selling 7's machinery — it resolves as a pricing error on one line), a credit note issued for the difference — which fixes the balance AND the VAT AND the statement AND the story, because the document carries all four where the journal carried none. The branch manager gets the explanation in one sentence: documents fix documents; journals can only fix journals.

The first monthly audit (Ch. 7). Close week: eleven journals in the month — seven recurring (scanned in a minute; the set ran), the correction pair (file complete, references clean), and two events (a director loan movement, evidenced and party-carried; a bank charge posted from the reconciliation with the statement referenced). One catch: the director-loan entry's remarks say only transfer as agreed — sent back for the story (which agreement, what evidence), rewritten in five minutes, the remarks law enforced on its first test. The audit takes eighteen minutes; the journal count — eleven — goes on the health page as its own quiet metric; and the manual layer ends its first month exactly as designed: small, storied, and boring.

lessons.title: Chapter 9 — Common mistakes & the second law
lessons.html:
The manual layer's scar tissue. Symptom → disease → fix.

Pattern 1 — the journal habit. Symptom: hundreds of journals monthly; sales and purchases journalised; the trading modules idle. Disease: the machine declined (Ch. 1) — old-instrument fluency never transferred, every total now detail-less. Fix: the document test applied to the whole traffic, the biggest categories migrated to their documents first (sales, then purchases, then payments), the fluency transfer taught with respect — and the journal count watched as the recovery's metric.

Pattern 2 — suspense parking. Symptom: the balancing side nobody could find, parked in suspense; the account growing monthly (module 1's squatter, now with its cause named). Disease: the one-sided instinct — the author posting what they know and warehousing the rest. Fix: the balance law taken seriously (the other side always exists — find it or don't post), the monthly sweep to zero, and the classification gaps fixed at their source.

Pattern 3 — the tie-breaker journals. Symptom: control accounts that stopped agreeing with parties; a stock bridge diverged by a suspiciously round number; a tax account that matches a filing but not its register. Disease: the forbidden list violated (Ch. 6) — totals adjusted around their details. Fix: the journal filter on the protected accounts (the fastest audit in accounting), each hit reversed and re-routed through its proper instrument, the fence re-taught, and the door narrowed.

Pattern 4 — the storyless journal. Symptom: entries whose remarks are empty, cryptic, or say adjustment; audits that stall on them; authors who cannot recall them. Disease: the remarks law unenforced (Ch. 2) — testimony without witnesses accumulating. Fix: the story required at entry (workflow where available, culture always), the monthly audit bouncing the storyless back, and the templates carrying their stories so the recurring traffic is never the problem.

Pattern 5 — the year-end journal storm. Symptom: a quiet ledger all year, then fifty journals in the close week — accruals never run monthly, corrections hoarded, the auditor's adjustments landing in one avalanche. Disease: the manual layer run annually instead of monthly (Ch. 4, 7) — every month's statements wrong all year, corrected once, when nobody remembers anything. Fix: the recurring set on its monthly rhythm, corrections posted when found (the doctrine's period rule), the monthly audit keeping the layer current — the storm dissolving into weather, which is this academy's oldest trade.

The second law. The first law made the chart the language and the ledger its testimony. The second governs the one pen that writes testimony directly: the journal is the exception and the document is the rule — what a document can do, a document must do; every journal carries its story; and the pen is held by two names behind a monthly audit. The lawful catalogue is real and small; the forbidden list defends every bridge three tracks built; the correction doctrine keeps history honest; and a healthy manual layer is exactly what HealthTrade's first month showed — small, storied, boring. Module 3 turns to the account the whole firm watches most: the bank, and the outside witness that keeps it honest.
